1 Wahrscheinlich für Alhazen (Ibn Heitham) der als Philosophus citirt zu
werden pflegt (s. Rose, Aristoteles Pseudepigr., p. 376); Steinschneider, l. c., p. 367,
§ 16 b.
2 De Tâbit ben Qorra, cf. supra p. 88, n. 4.
3 Celeberrimus est Ptolemaei Quadripartitus (cf. Catal., I, p. 4, etc.). Quamnam
veterum versionum Albertus inspexerit, frustra quaesivit Steinschneider, l. c.,
p. 383.
4 Albumasaris vel Aponiasaris (Abû-Ma‘shar Dja‘far ben Muhamed el Balchî)

sections.en:
1 Probably for Alhazen (Ibn Heitham) who is usually cited as Philosophus
(see Rose, Aristoteles Pseudepigr., p. 376); Steinschneider, l. c., p. 367,
§ 16 b.
2 On Tâbit ben Qorra, cf. above p. 88, n. 4.
3 Most famous is Ptolemy's Quadripartitus (cf. Catal., I, p. 4, etc.). Which
of the old versions Albertus inspected, Steinschneider sought in vain, l. c.,
p. 383.
4 Greek excerpts of Albumasar or Aponiasar (Abû-Ma‘shar Dja‘far ben Muhamed el Balchî)
will be edited below (from cod. 2). His Introductorium majus or Liber

summary.headline: Books of Judicial Astronomy
summary.text: Defense of astronomy and its books, followed by Chapter VI’s catalogue of works of judicial astronomy: Ptolemy’s Quadripartitus (Tetrastin/Abrabaha), including its section on nativities, and Jafar Albumasar’s Greater Introductorium. Authorities cited include Aristotle, Thābit ibn Qurra, and Alhazen.
